Hi @Komier! It's been 3 weeks since I've last checked this clash, and it's already looking much better. However, there are still some pain points that I'd like to address:

1) Long Statement:
The statement is crazy long; maybe even one of the longest statements I've seen on CoC. Long statements in fastest mode drive everyone nuts and usually encourages Googling the answer. 

These are the redundancies in your statement that I suggest removing:
***
When proofreading, some people have a hard time time seeing repeats, especially if they're broken up onto different lines. The brain just ignores them.
***
*** (You don't get access to this in Reverse anyway, so no point in explaining even further)
Example:
Input:
Example example text Text text , , a!a. a ,a hi! hi!
Output:
Example
text
hi!
Reasoning:
The first group of repeated words starts with "Example".
The second group of repeated words starts with "text".
The third group of repeats doesn't contain an alphabetical character, so isn't a word.
The fourth group differs by non-alphabetical characters.
The fifth group of "hi! hi!" is a repeat as every character is the same in each word.
***
You don't need Rule #1.

2) Complexity:
That's a lot of rules for one clash. I guess you could keep all your rules, but I recommend dropping a few to make this more "clash-friendly" in a way. My recommendation is to just avoid using \n and use spaces only.

3) Difficulty???
It took me over a day to finally get this, but maybe that's because I just suck :( - don't take it too seriously with this part

My solution:
s = input().replace("\\n"," ").split()
l = []
c = ""
n = 0
for w in s:
    if not any(i.isalpha() for i in w):
        continue
    if w.lower() == c.lower():
        n += 1
        if n == 2:
            l.append(c)
    else:
        n = 1
        c = w
if not l:
    print("No repeats!")
else:
    for i in l:
        print(i)

Idea is good.
Can be solved within 5min.
Test cases are good.
but you can work on description + in your example there was three repeated words text Text text. you are checking in terms of pair, you should remove this part instead you should return one word even if it is repeating many times, because in you goal you said it is to make proof reading easy so this will match your goal

This clash is a bit confusing for me because in your example case, 'Example' and 'example' are considered repeats, but 'text', 'Text', and 'text' (I'm assuming you drop the period at the end) get 2 repeats: 'text' and 'Text'. I don't feel like your statement clearly explains that part yet.

I agree that the current statement is confusing. Several rules are either missing or inconsistently applied across the cases.

Goal
* The statement does not clearly define what counts as a "word" or how digits, spaces, punctuations and other symbols should be handled.

* The statement does not mention that the string "\n" (backslash + n) may appear in the input and should be treated as a newline instead. It also does not explain how newlines should affect word separation.

* The statement does not specify whether repeated words must be consecutive or may appear anywhere in the text. For example, Test 4 shows non-adjacent duplicates ("might" and "it's") being detected across intervening line breaks.

* The statement does not clarify whether each duplicate should be printed once per repeated occurrence or once per repeated word overall.

Solution
* Your solution does not handle punctuations and symbols consistently.

  - Example 1: In Test 1: your solution treats "text Text text." as containing two repeated words: "text" and "Text". However, in Validator 3, it treats "lie lie, lie." as containing only one repeated word: "lie".

  - Example 2: In Validator 3, your solution recognises "lie" as repeated for the input "lie lie, lie.". However, if the input is reordered to "lie, lie. lie", your solution no longer recognises "lie" as repeated.

  - Example 3: In Test 4, your solution recognises "it's" as repeated. But if the second occurrence is changed to "it's'", the trailing apostrophe is removed and the word is still treated as "it's", because your solution always strips a final character that's not a letter.

  - Example 4: In contrast, variants such as "it's''", "'it's" or "it's!?!", aren't recognised as equivalent to "it's".

  (I know some of the examples above aren't valid English usage, but that shouldn't matter here, especially since the existing test cases already contain similar inputs such as "run*nrun" and "jump!jump".)

* Your solution treats all punctuations and symbols that aren't in the final position as part of the word itself. So it interprets "it's", "run*nrun" and "jump!jump" as 3 words instead of 5.

Other comments:

Goal
* Please format "No repeats!" as a {{constant}}.

Output
* Please mention {{No repeats!}} as a possible output.

Cases
* Each test and its validator should cover the same scenario with slightly different inputs. Currently, Test 3 is the only case expecting "No repeats!", while Validator 3 contains repeated words, so the two cases aren't aligned.

* The above point is especially important since the Reverse mode for the clash has been enabled.

Thanks.

I thought about that, and went with what I'm doing now because it seemed more useful as a "tool" to edit my stuff. But having more than 1 person suggesting that, I can make it so you only take the first word in any string of repeats.

A lot of the length is due to problems with ambiguity. I'll post a modified statement at the bottom of this comment, if it's not too ambiguous, I can use that one instead.

I figured it wasn't too hard, since I've run into clashes I didn't even understand, clashes I couldn't code within 15 minutes, clashes I knew exactly what they wanted while still not knowing how to code it, and reverse clashes I never figured out. I would say this may be only at the level of an "Easy" puzzle at its hardest, so it could work. On the time it takes to code it, I'm probably not able to judge it since I made it, but my original version took me about 15 minutes, and the current version is a little easier.

Here's the proposed modified statement:

Print all of the <<consecutively repeated>> words found in a string, one on each line.

For the purposes of this clash, a <<word>> is defined thus:
1) <<Words>> are separated by spaces and/or {{\n}} (backslash + n).
2) <<Words>> must contain at least one alphabetical character.

Rules:
1) Ignore capitalization when comparing.
2) When outputting repeats, print the first <<word>> as it originally appears.
3) If there are many consecutive repeats, print only the first <<word>>.
4) Print each repeated <<word>> on its own line, in the order found.
5) If there are no repeats, write {{No repeats!}}.

Example:

Input:
Example example text Text text , , a!a. a ,a hi! hi!

Output:
Example
text
hi!

Could you please clarify this point?
"You don't get access to this in Reverse anyway, so no point in explaining even further"

The clash has other modes enabled too.

@5DN1L: In Reverse mode, you don't have access to the statement. So in favor of shortening the statement, I would get rid of the explanation of the example as the rules section is already sufficient in explaining it. Leaving it would just make fastest and shortest modes a handicap in a way.

@Komier: And this was my suggestion of a shorter statement if you are interested in it:
Print all <<consecutively repeated>> words found in [[string]] on each line.

<<Words are defined as:>>
<<1)>> Words are separated by <<spaces>> or line breaks, represented by {{\n}} (backslash + n).
<<2)>> Words <<MUST>> contain at least one <<alphabetical character>>.
<<3)>> Count all <<non-alphabetical characters>> as part of the word. (E.g. it's)

<<Rules:>>
<<1)>> Ignore capitalization when comparing.
<<2)>> For each set of repeats, print <<only>> the <<first>> word <<exactly>> as it originally appears.
<<3)>> Print each repeated word on its own line, in the order found.
<<4)>> If there are no repeats, write {{No repeats!}}.

Ok, I think I've addressed these issues. Unfortunately, the new constraints push the time it would take me to code this past the guideline of 5 minutes. I could probably do this in a clash, but unlike the previous iteration, I'm not sure I could finish it fast enough.  Let me know if I should make it easier instead.
I would suggest restricting non-letter characters in the input to spaces and "\n" only, for simplicity.
Are you still planning to modify the contribution? If so, please change the status to WIP first to prevent accidental approval. Thank you.
Sorry, I didn't realize it wasn't set to WIP.

No worries.

Once you've finished all the changes, just drop me a message here, and I'll be happy to take another look 🙂

Ok, I've made the changes requested. Now it requires that you count all of the repeated words, and only output the first of them. I had to redo the solution; didn't know a more clever way to handle it than manually controlling the index. Sorry about the low readability.

I did make the statement a little more clear, I think.

The expanded rules clarify some aspects, but other aspects are still quite confusing.

Goal
* Currently, "\n" is shown without explicitly stating that this refers to the two-character sequence "backslash + n" rather than an actual line break. Players may not realise this until they inspect the test cases and expected outputs.

* The rules are still unclear about how words are defined and how special characters should be treated.

Using the example "a , a!a. a ,a":

1. Separate the tokens by spaces:
"a", ",", "a!a.", "a" ",a".

2. Ignore leading or trailing non-letters:
"a", ",", "a!a", "a", "a".

(a) Should the comma (the original second token) be treated as a "non-alphabetical character at the start or end of a word"?

(b) You explain that this group "is separated by special characters so isn't included". Are you referring to the comma mentioned in (a)?

(c) Is "a!a" a word? I'd expect it to be, since inputs like "it's" and "shouldn't" are treated as words in the test cases.

(d) The group ends with "a" and "a", which appears to form a repeated group. Are the rules "ignore non-alphabetical character at the start or end of a word" and "special characters between words" in conflict here, if the latter is the reason for the two "a"s *not* to be considered as a repeated group?

(e) The statement says to ignore non-letters at the start or end of a word, but also says to print the first word exactly as it originally appears. Are those leading/trailing non-letters considered part of the word or not?

Constraints
* 2nd constraint: I think the current example is overly complicated and not focused enough to illustrate the rule clearly. Consider simplifying it by removing the first two question marks.

* 3rd constraint: This needs rewording. As written, it effectively says "some characters won't contain other characters", which doesn't make sense.

Cases
* I understand that:
  - Test/Validator 1 is the example pair,
  - Test/Validator 3 is the "No repeats!" scenario.

  However, the objectives or scenarios covered by the other case pairs are unclear.
  
  Please rearrange and/or modify the cases so that each pair targets a specific rule or edge case. For example:
  
  - one pair for handling \n,
  - one pair for non-letters inside words,
  - one pair for capitalisation,
  - a final comprehensive pair covering all rules together.

* After that, include a short summary in the comment section here describing the purpose of each test/validator pair.

Thanks.

I just made it simpler to avoid having to manage a growing summary when I already found mistakes introduced by editing, which is amusing as this was originally a puzzle about editing mistakes.

Test 1: example
Test 2: Handle '\n' instead of only spaces.
Test 3: Print only one repeat if more than two consecutively
Test 4: Handle differing capitalization.
Test 5: Non-alphabetical characters are considered part of the word leading to "No repeats!"
Test 6: Handle edge case of repeats being the first and the last word.
Test 7: Several at once.

Comment part 1 of 2 (split due to character limit)

Goal
* Great improvement in the clarity of the rules! Here are a few suggestions to make them even clearer:

1) Change "one input string" to "one line of input". I think the latter better conveys your intended meaning.

2) Change "line breaks (backslash+n) {{\n}}" to "line breaks. Line breaks are always represented as {{\n}} (backslash + n) in this clash."

4) Change 'E.g. "it's" is equivalent to "it's"' to "Example: {{it's}}".

5) Change "there are multiple repeated words" to "a word is repeated multiple times".

* Consider formatting "Example:" in <<bold>>. You could also format important keywords in <<bold>> if that helps players follow the rules more easily.

* Move the "No repeats!" sentence into the numbered rules as Rule 8. Right now it reads more like part of the example than an actual rule.

Inputs
* Please add "[[string]]" after "string".

Constraints
* Please remove the second constraint. It contains some of the rules rather than actual constraints.

* Please change "Input string" to "[[string]]".

* Please add:
1 ≤ length of [[string]] ≤ 256

Solution
* Your solution still uses is.alpha(), which seems unnecessary given the revised rules. Here's my solution for reference:

string = input()

string = string.replace("\\n", " ")

prev_word = ""
prev_repeat = ""
answer = []
for curr_word in string.split():
    curr_word_lower = curr_word.lower()
    if prev_word.lower() == curr_word_lower:
        if prev_repeat != curr_word_lower:
            prev_repeat = curr_word_lower
            answer.append(prev_word)
    else:
        prev_repeat = ""
    prev_word = curr_word

if answer:
    print(*answer, sep = "\n")
else:
    print("No repeats!")

In problems like this, it's usually fine to use a single loop together with one or more previous-value holders to compare elements in a sliding-window style, without first determining the number of elements.

Comment part 2 of 2

Cases
* Please renumber Test 7 and Validator 7 as Test 8 and Validator 8. A new case pair will then be inserted before them (see the next point). ALTERNATIVELY, add a constraint stating that the same word cannot appear in more than one repeated group.

* Please add a new Pair 7 where the same word appears in several consecutive repeated groups:

(from https://jwed.co.uk/2020/03/28/flowers-of-rhetoric-epizeuxis )

We've got egg, bacon, sausage and spam; spam, bacon, sausage and spam; spam, egg, spam, spam, bacon and spam; spam, spam, spam, egg and spam; spam, spam, spam, spam, spam, spam, baked beans, spam, spam, spam and spam

(from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_linguistic_example_sentences#Lexical_ambiguity ):

Fish and and, and and and And, and And and and, and and and And, and And and and, and and and Chips

* " \n " in part of a repeated group currently appears in Test 2 only. Please add the same feature to Validator 2.

* Additions to make Test 8 comprehensive:
  - " \n " inside a repeated group
  - different capitalization in a repeated group
  - the same word appearing in multiple repeated groups (not necessarily consecutively; irrelevant if this behaviour is disallowed)

* Additions to make Validator 8 comprehensive:
  - " \n " inside a repeated group
  - special character in a repeated word
  - a word repeated more than twice in the same group
  - the same word appearing in multiple repeated groups (not necessarily consecutively; irrelevant if this behaviour is disallowed)

Thanks.
Ok, I think I've addressed all of your concerns here. Test 7 requires that you output the same word more than once if it shows up in separate groups.

This version is looking good overall, and I only have a couple of minor suggestions left.

Goal
* Consider formatting "consecutively repeated" in <<bold>> because it's a key part of the task but could be easily overlooked.

* Rule 6: Please change "first word" to "first occurrence" for clarity. (Even with this change, the rule may still be ambiguous, but let's see what others think.)

Constraints
* Please delete "Input".

* Please add "including at least one alphabetical character" after "ASCII characters".

Thanks.

I think the constraint of only ASCII characters is sufficient. It doesn't matter what characters there are, as long as it doesn't explicitly repeat and matches rules 2-5 which define a word. For example, if the input was simply "! !" the result would obviously be "No repeats!" as a group can only count as a word when matching rule 3.

I'll include that as a test case to make it clearer.

Perhaps I should include a section that "defines" word for the purpose of this puzzle. That might make it clearer. I'll add that, let me know if you think it's better or worse. In this case, maybe I could bold every time I use the word 'word' to signal that I mean this special 'token' I've defined here, which could remove some ambiguity.

Your approach works as well. The new definition section is a strong improvement.

I don't have any further comments at the moment, so we can wait and see whether other reviewers have any additional suggestions or observations.
